plan: Ten new items; ideas that matched existing items (committee-report WIC, audiobook data, composting, desert ants, hummingbirds, shade) were replaced before drafting: ephemeral/restrained WIC, cicada sentence function, star-dip inference, litter percent-change data (hard), scribe cross-text, plural noun, colon, 'Nonetheless,', refill-station recommendation.

passages.title: Brief blooms
passages.text: Some desert wildflowers are strikingly ______: after a rare heavy rain they sprout, bloom, and drop their seeds within a few weeks, then disappear from the landscape until the next downpour, which may be years away.

passages.title: A cautious announcement
passages.text: In interviews about her team's discovery, the astronomer's tone was notably ______: she called the result "interesting" rather than "groundbreaking" and repeatedly stressed how much remained unknown.

passages.title: Safety in numbers
passages.text: Periodical cicadas in parts of North America spend 13 or 17 years underground as nymphs and then emerge by the millions within a few weeks. This timing is not a coincidence. Birds and other predators can eat only a small fraction of such an enormous swarm, so most of the cicadas survive long enough to mate, a strategy biologists call predator satiation.

passages.title: A regular dip
passages.text: Astronomers observing a distant star found that its brightness dropped by the same small amount every 12.4 days, with each dip lasting about three hours. Random changes on a star's surface do not repeat on such a precise schedule. The astronomers therefore concluded that ______

passages.title: Litter by type
passages.text:
Volunteers counted the litter collected during an annual beach cleanup. The town banned single-use plastic bags in 2022.
Litter type | 2021 | 2023
Plastic bottles | 420 | 210
Cigarette butts | 650 | 600
Plastic bags | 300 | 90
A local report claims that, from 2021 to 2023, plastic bags showed the largest percentage decrease of any litter type in the table.

passages.title: One hand or two? (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A historian argues that a fourteenth-century manuscript of sermons was copied entirely by a single scribe, citing the remarkably consistent shape of the letters from the first page to the last.

Text 2
Scribes trained in the same workshop were taught to imitate a single house style so closely that their hands can be hard to tell apart. In this manuscript, analysis of the parchment shows that the last third was made from animal skins prepared differently from those used in the first two-thirds.

passages.title: Mountain pastures
passages.text: Each spring, the ______ of the valley drive their goats up to the high pastures, where the animals graze until the first snow.

passages.title: Above all
passages.text: The expedition's success depended on one thing more than any other ______ the weather in the narrow window when the pass would be free of ice.

passages.title: Inefficient but indispensable
passages.text: The earliest steam engines were enormously inefficient, turning only a tiny fraction of the energy in their fuel into useful work. ______ they transformed mining in eighteenth-century Britain, because they could pump water out of deep mines far faster than teams of horses could.

passages.title: Refill stations
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2023, Ridgeview High School installed four water-bottle refill stations.
• Sales of bottled water in Ridgeview's cafeteria fell by 40 percent that year.
• Each station cost about $1,500 to install.
• The district's two other high schools have no refill stations.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: within a few weeks, then disappear from the landscape
candidates.explanation: Plants that sprout, bloom and vanish within weeks are "ephemeral": short-lived.

A.rationale: "Perennial" describes plants that live for many years, the opposite of plants that vanish within weeks.

B.rationale: "Dormant" means inactive; these flowers are described during a burst of rapid growth.

D.rationale: "Invasive" describes species that spread aggressively into new areas, which the text does not discuss.

hints: How long do these flowers last above ground?
candidates.remember: Use the time details to define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: she called the result "interesting" rather than "groundbreaking"
candidates.explanation: Choosing a modest word and stressing what is unknown shows a "restrained" tone.

A.rationale: Calling a result merely "interesting" and stressing unknowns is the opposite of boasting.

C.rationale: She does not dismiss the discovery; she describes it cautiously.

hints: Does she exaggerate or understate the discovery?
candidates.remember: Tone words must fit every detail in the explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole? (The underlined sentence is "This timing is not a coincidence.")

choices.A: It signals that the text will explain why the cicadas emerge together.
choices.B: It questions whether cicadas really emerge in large numbers.
choices.C: It introduces a second species of cicada that behaves differently.
choices.D: It concludes the text by summarizing the evidence presented.

candidates.evidence: This timing is not a coincidence.
candidates.explanation: After describing the synchronized emergence, the sentence announces that it has a cause, which the next sentence explains (predator satiation).

B.rationale: The text affirms the mass emergence; the sentence does not question it.

D.rationale: It comes in the middle and is followed by the explanation.

hints: What does the sentence after it explain?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the sentence sets up.

candidates.remember: Short sentences often announce what comes next.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the star's brightness changes randomly from one day to the next.
choices.B: the star is likely to stop shining within a few years.
choices.C: Earth's atmosphere causes the dips in the star's light.
choices.D: an object, likely a planet, regularly passes between the star and Earth.

candidates.evidence: Random changes on a star's surface do not repeat on such a precise schedule
candidates.explanation: A dip of the same size on a precise schedule, which surface changes cannot explain, points to something orbiting the star and blocking part of its light at regular intervals.

A.rationale: The text says the dips repeat on a precise schedule, which rules out randomness.

B.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns the star's lifespan.

C.rationale: Atmospheric effects would not repeat exactly every 12.4 days for one star.

hints: What kind of event repeats on an exact schedule?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate explanations the text rules out.

candidates.remember: Regular repetition suggests an orbit or cycle, not chance.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the report's claim?

choices.A: Bags fell 70 percent; bottles fell 50 percent and butts about 8 percent.
choices.B: Plastic bags and plastic bottles each decreased by 210 items from 2021 to 2023.
choices.C: Cigarette butts were the most common type of litter in both 2021 and 2023.
choices.D: Only 90 plastic bags were collected in 2023, fewer than any other type.

candidates.evidence: plastic bags showed the largest percentage decrease of any litter type
candidates.explanation: Bags fell from 300 to 90 (70 percent), bottles from 420 to 210 (50 percent) and cigarette butts from 650 to 600 (about 8 percent). Only A compares percentage decreases.

B.rationale: Equal raw decreases do not show which percentage decrease was largest; in fact they suggest a tie.

C.rationale: This concerns which type was most common, not the size of each decrease.

D.rationale: The smallest 2023 count does not by itself show the largest percentage decrease.

hints: Does the claim compare raw numbers or percentages?
candidates.remember: Percent claims need percent evidence; raw changes can mislead.

author_checklist.hardness: Choice B is tempting because it uses accurate figures, but equal raw decreases of 210 hide very different percentage changes (70 vs. 50 percent); students must compute percentages.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historian's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the consistent handwriting proves a single scribe copied the manuscript
choices.B: By arguing that the manuscript was copied in a later century than the historian claims
choices.C: By noting that consistent letter shapes might reflect a shared workshop style rather than one scribe
choices.D: By claiming that the manuscript's sermons were written by several different authors

candidates.evidence: taught to imitate a single house style so closely that their hands can be hard to tell apart
candidates.explanation: Text 2 undercuts the handwriting evidence by explaining that workshop-trained scribes wrote alike, and it adds parchment evidence that the last third may have been made separately.

A.rationale: Text 2 explains why consistent handwriting may not prove a single scribe.

B.rationale: Text 2 does not dispute the date.

D.rationale: Text 2 is about who copied the manuscript, not who wrote the sermons.

hints: Why might handwriting look consistent even with more than one scribe?

strategy.explanation: Find what Text 2 says about handwriting.

candidates.remember: A response often challenges the evidence, not just the conclusion.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: drive their goats up to the high pastures
candidates.explanation: The word is the plural subject of "drive" and possesses nothing directly after it ("of the valley" follows), so no apostrophe is needed.

A.rationale: The apostrophe makes a singular possessive, but the word is the subject and possesses nothing here.

C.rationale: The apostrophe makes a plural possessive, but nothing follows that the herders possess.

hints: Does the word own anything that immediately follows it?

strategy.explanation: Use an apostrophe only to show possession.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The expedition's success depended on one thing more than any other
candidates.explanation: A complete clause that anticipates something ("one thing more than any other") is followed by a colon introducing that thing: the weather.

A.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "the weather ..." is a noun phrase.

B.rationale: A comma here makes the phrase read as a loosely attached afterthought; a colon is needed to introduce the thing named.

hints: Is the part before the blank a complete sentence that sets something up?

strategy.explanation: Rule out marks that need a clause on both sides.

candidates.remember: Use a colon after a complete clause to introduce what it announces.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The engines succeeded despite being inefficient, so a transition signaling contrast with an expectation, "Nonetheless," fits.

B.rationale: Inefficiency is not a reason the engines transformed mining.

C.rationale: The second sentence is not similar to the first; it describes success despite a weakness.

D.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of inefficiency.

hints: Would you expect an inefficient machine to transform an industry?
candidates.remember: "Nonetheless" introduces a result that happens despite what came before.

candidates.stem: The student wants to recommend an action to the school district. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Ridgeview High School installed four water-bottle refill stations in 2023, at about $1,500 each.
choices.B: The district's two other high schools do not currently have any water-bottle refill stations.
choices.C: Given Ridgeview's 40 percent drop in bottled-water sales, the district should add stations at its other high schools.
choices.D: Sales of bottled water in Ridgeview's cafeteria fell by 40 percent in 2023, the year stations were installed.

candidates.evidence: The district's two other high schools have no refill stations.
candidates.explanation: Only C makes a recommendation (install stations at the other schools) and supports it with relevant evidence from the notes.

A.rationale: This reports facts but recommends no action.

B.rationale: This states a fact without a recommendation.

D.rationale: This presents a result but does not recommend anything.

hints: Which choice tells the district what to do?

strategy.explanation: The goal asks for a recommendation.

candidates.remember: A recommendation says what should be done and why.
